transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Ava (Redwood AE), Jasper (Redwood SE), Oliver (Mariner CTO), Priya (Head of Platform), Marcus (SRE), Tess (Product)

[00:00] Ava: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Ava from Redwood Inference, and with me is Jasper our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Oliver: Good, thanks. Busy week but we set time aside to talk through dedicated capacity — super important for our product roadmap.
[00:12] Priya: Hi all. We're especially focused on isolation and predictable throughput.
[00:15] Jasper: Great, we'll run through questions and try to size what dedicated looks like. Quick ask — can you share the rough QPS and typical prompt lengths up front?
[00:24] Marcus: Sure, I can say ballpark. Right now production is running about 80 RPS for our main inference endpoint, but peaks to 220 RPS during batch processing at the top of the hour. Average prompt length is around 350 tokens, responses about 180 tokens.
[00:38] Tess: And a lot of those are multi-turn chat sessions for our advisor product. Latency target is <200ms 95th for interactive flows.
[00:47] Ava: Good — that gives us a starting point. Are you running anything on-prem or is it all cloud?
[00:52] Oliver: Mostly AWS — EKS clusters, some EC2 GPU instances for prototyping. We're evaluating Dedicated so that we get reserved GPUs and stronger isolation than the hosted API. Compliance is a big driver for us — SOC 2 plus client data residency concerns.
[01:07] Jasper: Got it. For dedicated we provide reserved GPU pools that can be VPC-isolated or part of a private control plane for our Private offering. For Dedicated the control plane is still managed but you get capacity isolation and an SLA.
[01:19] Priya: Can you explain the burst strategy? We have spiky traffic — sometimes a nightly job will enqueue lots of requests; we don't want throttling or high queue times.
[01:27] Jasper: Absolutely. Two common patterns: one is reserved capacity sized for steady-state with a burst buffer in the cloud for temporary overflow, second is policy-based autoscaling within the dedicated pool. We support configurable burst bands — essentially you pre-commit X GPUs and allow burst to a higher tier with overage pricing or from shared pool if you enable it. Note: the behavior depends on contract and region.
[01:47] Marcus: Do we need to provision a separate VPC peering or can Redwood sit inside our VPC? We have tight network egress policies.
[01:55] Ava: For Dedicated we usually set up a VPC peering or private link; for Private we can provide a customer-hosted control plane and fully air-gapped options. We'll share a network diagram.
[02:05] Oliver: K, that helps. On sizing, with 220 RPS peaks, 350 token prompts, 180 token outputs — what's the GPU sizing ballpark?
[02:15] Jasper: Quick rough calc: peak tokens per second = 220 * (350+180) ≈ 96,600 tokens/sec — sorry, that's tokens per second if requests are entirely parallel which they aren't. Let me reframe: if average throughput is 80 RPS sustained, that's ~42k tokens/sec distributed. Key factors: model family (LLM size), sequence length, batching efficiency, KV cache hit rates, and quantization. What model are you planning to serve?
[02:39] Oliver: We're testing a mix of open models mostly 13B variants right now; potentially moving to a tuned 70B for higher quality later.
[02:46] Jasper: For 13B with 350 in/180 out you should get much higher tokens/sec per GPU vs 70B. With continuous batching and prefix cache, a single A100 or H100-equivalent can handle several hundred RPS depending on latency SLOs. I can run a tighter sizing model after we see your exact token histograms.
[03:03] Priya: What's Redwood's approach to caching? We have many repeated prompts and a lot of shared prefixes.
[03:07] Jasper: We do prefix/KV caching across requests which dramatically reduces compute for repeated prefixes. We also support configurable cache TTLs, and shard-aware cache placement for Dedicated pools. Those are tunable with your workload.
[03:17] Ava: Also worth calling out quantization: running 4-bit or 8-bit variants can shift how many GPUs you need. That might be reasonable for 13B models.
[03:24] Marcus: Any specifics on SLA and failover? If a GPU node fails during a run, what's the behavior?
[03:29] Jasper: Our Dedicated offering has an SLA for availability and latency tiers. Runtime does graceful fallback — if a node fails we can route to another node or fall back to a hosted-compatible variant if you enable cross-fallback. For strict isolation you might not want automatic fallback to hosted; that's configurable.
[03:43] Oliver: I like that. Security — do you integrate with our KMS? We require CMEK for keys and want audit logs forwarded to our SIEM.
[03:52] Ava: Yes, we support customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) for Private and Dedicated enterprise plans, plus audit logs and integrations with Splunk/Datadog. We'll attach the SOC2 and security whitepaper.
[04:02] Priya: Data residency — some clients mandate that data never leaves EU. Can Dedicated be pinned to region?
[04:07] Jasper: Yes, you can pin capacity to regions. For full EU-only custody we'd recommend Private deployment or dedicated regional pools with contractual clauses.
[04:16] Tess: About pricing — reserved capacity vs pay-as-you-go — what's the typical model?
[04:20] Ava: Reserved capacity is usually monthly or annual commit for GPU counts, with discounts for longer commitments. Burst capacity and overage are billed at higher unit rates. We'll send the pricing and a sizing spreadsheet that models cost for different commit levels.
[04:33] Marcus: For benchmarking, what do you need from us to run a realistic test?
[04:36] Jasper: We'll need traffic histograms (per-minute RPS distribution), sample prompts representative of multi-turn flows, expected percentiles for latency, and any auth/role flows that impact request routing. We can run a benchmark on our dedicated staging cluster or on your staging VPC depending on access.
[04:51] Oliver: We can share traffic logs and a 48-hour sample. Are there any gotchas we should expect moving from our self-hosted prototypes?
[04:58] Jasper: Common ones: naive batching can blow latency targets if not tuned; model quantization can change output variance so you'll want evals on quality; and network egress / VPC setup can add latency if not colocated. We'll help run tuning and provide recommended autoscale policies.
[05:14] Priya: On autoscale, is the scaling based on tokens/sec, RPS, or GPU utilization?
[05:19] Jasper: We support policy triggers on multiple signals — RPS, token throughput, and GPU utilization. For latency SLOs we recommend hybrid: maintain a baseline GPU pool and trigger scale based on queue depth and 95th latency breaches.
[05:30] Ava: Quick clarification — do you need guaranteed single-tenant hardware (no co-located customers) or is logical isolation via reserved pools sufficient?
[05:38] Oliver: For now logical isolation + VPC peering is OK, but some clients might require single-tenant in the future. Want to understand path to Private.
[05:45] Jasper: Private is the path for single-tenant/on-prem. We can migrate you from Dedicated to Private if needed; there are additional fees and deployment steps.
[05:52] Tess: Any examples of other fintech customers with similar needs?
[05:55] Ava: We have a few references — banks and trading platforms using Dedicated with reserved pools and burst policies. I'll share anonymized case studies.
[06:02] Oliver: Perfect. One more technical — what about KV cache warmup time for multi-turn sessions when customers jump between flows?
[06:09] Jasper: If you have sticky sessions we can maintain KV caches per session; otherwise cold starts will pay the initial token cost. We do prefix similarity detection to accelerate warmups.
[06:18] Marcus: Ok thanks.
[06:20] Ava: Let's recap next steps. We'll send pricing & sizing spreadsheet, SOC2/security docs, and a network diagram. Jasper will prepare a benchmark plan. You (Oliver) will share traffic histograms and sample prompts. We'll aim to run a benchmark in your staging VPC the week of March 16.
[06:35] Oliver: Sounds good. One ask — can you also include a cost comparison for running 13B quantized vs 70B in small fleet for quality tradeoffs?
[06:43] Jasper: Yeah, we'll include that in the sizing spreadsheet and run some rough cost/perf tradeoffs.
[06:48] Priya: Great. Thanks everyone.
[06:50] Ava: Thanks — we'll follow up by Friday.
[06:53] (call ends)

Notes about transcript quality: automatic transcription had occasional speaker misattributions, a few proper nouns (e.g., H100) were transcribed as 'H-one-hundred' or 'H one hundred' and 'Triton' as 'try-ton' in places. Some timestamps approximate.
